Detection and Visualization of Cold Waves

INMET Pipeline → Gap-filling → Indicators → Cold Waves | sus_climate_compute_coldwaves() and sus_climate_plot_coldwaves()

Dr. Max Anjos

17 September, 2026

Source: vignettes/ondas_de_frio.Rmd
ondas_de_frio.Rmd

Introduction

Cold waves are extreme climatic events frequently underestimated on Brazil’s public health agenda. Although Brazil is known for its warm climate, the South and Southeast regions experience periodic episodes of intense cold associated with the penetration of Atlantic polar air masses, causing excess cardiovascular and respiratory mortality — particularly among the elderly, children, and outdoor workers (Gasparrini et al., 2015; Huynen et al., 2001). Global studies estimate that the risk attributable to cold exceeds that of heat in many regions, including subtropical zones (Gasparrini et al., 2015).

In Rio Grande do Sul, polar cold fronts can reduce temperature by 10–15 °C in less than 24 hours during the austral winter (June–August). In Porto Alegre, episodes with minimum temperatures below 5 °C frequently last 5 to 10 consecutive days, imposing an additional burden on the respiratory and cardiovascular systems of vulnerable populations. The absence of cold-wave surveillance systems comparable to those for heat waves contributes to this risk remaining underdiagnosed in SUS analyses.

climasus4r implements seven internationally recognized methodologies for cold-wave detection, following the same pipeline structure already available for heat waves. This tutorial demonstrates the complete pipeline from INMET data download to interactive visualization of the results, using the Porto Alegre station (A801) as a case study.

Note on reproducibility: The entire pipeline is deterministic — given the same INMET data period and the same parameters, results are identical across runs. Code blocks marked with eval = FALSE require an internet connection for the download step (INMET) and may take a few minutes depending on the requested period.

What is a cold wave?

Like heat waves, cold waves are defined by two components:

  1. Temperature threshold — the temperature (or thermal comfort index) must fall below a certain critical value, typically defined as a low percentile of the historical distribution (P10, P5) or as a fixed negative deviation from the climatological mean. While heat waves use the upper tail (P90), cold waves use the lower tail (P10).
  2. Minimum duration — the extreme condition must persist for at least N consecutive days (commonly 3 or 5 days), distinguishing sustained events from isolated temperature drops.

The absence of a universal definition reflects regional variability in climate and physiological tolerance thresholds. The INMET criterion for cold, for example, uses an absolute deviation of −5 °C from the historical minimum temperature (Tmin − 5 °C), rather than the maximum temperature used in the heat-wave criterion.

Why compare methods? In subtropical regions such as Rio Grande do Sul, the INMET method — calibrated for national climatic conditions using minimum temperature — tends to detect events that generic percentiles may not capture in atypically cold years. The ECF (Excess Cold Factor, the cold analogue of the EHF) is the only method that accounts for the acclimatization factor: the same minimum temperature is physiologically more stressful when it occurs after a relatively warm period, because the body has not had time to adapt to the cold. Comparing the seven methods is good sensitivity-analysis practice.

Pipeline overview

1. sus_climate_inmet() → 2. sus_climate_fill_inmet() → 3. sus_climate_compute_indicators() → 4. sus_climate_compute_coldwaves() → 5. sus_climate_plot_coldwaves()

Each step receives the output of the previous one and adds information. The function sus_climate_compute_coldwaves() expects hourly data with standardized temperature and thermal comfort index columns — exactly what sus_climate_compute_indicators() produces.

Environment setup 

# Instalar climasus4r (GitHub) se necessário
# install.packages("remotes")
# remotes::install_github("MaxAnjos/climasus4r")

library(climasus4r)
library(dplyr)

Optional dependencies: The visualization functions require ggplot2, ggsci, and plotly. For interactive plots, also install htmlwidgets. The climate indicators step requires slider (sliding windows) and jsonlite.

install.packages(c("ggplot2", "ggsci", "plotly", "htmlwidgets", "slider", "jsonlite"))

Step 1 — Acquiring climate data (INMET)

The INMET station network

The National Institute of Meteorology (INMET) operates Brazil’s largest automatic weather station network, with coverage in every state. Data are made available in CSV format at hourly resolution and include air temperature (dry bulb, maximum, minimum), relative humidity, wind speed and direction, atmospheric pressure, and precipitation.

The function sus_climate_inmet() automates the download, parsing, and standardization of these files into an analysis-ready format.

Main parameters 

# Estrutura da chamada completa
df_inmet <- sus_climate_inmet(
  years        = 2020:2023,   # Vetor de anos
  uf           = "",        # UF (sigla) para filtrar estações
  station_code = NULL,        # Código(s) específico(s) de estação (opcional)
  use_cache    = TRUE,        # Reutilizar arquivos já baixados
  cache_dir    = "~/.climasus4r_cache/climate",
  parallel     = FALSE,       # TRUE habilita download paralelo via furrr/future
  workers      = NULL,        # NULL = detectar automaticamente via parallelly
  lang         = "pt",
  verbose      = TRUE
)
Parameter Type Description
years integer or vector Years to download (e.g., 2020:2023)
uf character State abbreviation to filter stations (e.g., "RS", "SC")
station_code character Specific INMET station code(s) (e.g., "A801")
use_cache logical If TRUE, reuses files already downloaded in cache_dir
parallel logical Enables parallel download via furrr/future (requires multiple cores)
workers integer or NULL Number of workers; NULL auto-detects via parallelly

Example: Porto Alegre (RS) station

In this tutorial, we use data from the automatic Porto Alegre station (INMET code A801), in Rio Grande do Sul — the state with the largest historical record of cold waves in Brazil. Porto Alegre, at a latitude of approximately −30°S, is subject to regular penetration of Atlantic polar air masses during the austral winter, making it a natural laboratory for the study of extreme cold events.

# Download de dados horários (2020–2023)
# A primeira execução pode levar alguns minutos; execuções subsequentes usam cache.
df_inmet <- sus_climate_inmet(
  years        = 2020:2023,
  uf = "RS",   # Porto Alegre - RS
  use_cache    = TRUE,
  parallel     = FALSE,    # Use TRUE com workers = NULL em máquinas multicore
  lang         = "pt",
  verbose      = TRUE
)

# Inspecionar estrutura
glimpse(df_inmet)

The output is a data.frame at hourly resolution with columns standardized by climasus4r:

#> Rows: ~35,064  (4 anos x 365 dias x 24 horas)
#>  Columns: ~20
#> 
#>  $ date               <POSIXct>  2020-01-01 00:00:00, 2020-01-01 01:00:00 ...
#>  $ station_code       <chr>      'A801', 'A801', ...
#>  $ station_name       <chr>      'PORTO ALEGRE', 'PORTO ALEGRE', ...
#>  $ federal_unit       <chr>      'RS', 'RS', ...
#>  $ region             <chr>      'Sul', 'Sul', ...
#>  $ latitude           <dbl>      -30.05, -30.05, ...
#>  $ longitude          <dbl>      -51.17, -51.17, ...
#>  $ tair_dry_bulb_c    <dbl>      14.2, 13.8, ...
#>  $ tair_max_c         <dbl>      16.1, 15.4, ...
#>  $ tair_min_c         <dbl>      12.5, 12.1, ...
#>  $ rh_pct             <dbl>      78.0, 80.0, ...
#>  $ wind_speed_ms      <dbl>      2.1, 1.8, ...
#>  $ precip_mm          <dbl>      0.0, 0.0, ...

Data source: The raw data are the CSV files made publicly available by INMET at https://portal.inmet.gov.br/dadoshistoricos. climasus4r automatically parses each annual file, applies quality control, and standardizes the column names. No interpolation or modification of values is performed at this stage.

Step 2 — Gap-filling

The problem of gaps in hourly series

INMET automatic stations frequently show gaps caused by transmission failures, equipment maintenance, or extreme weather events. The presence of missing values (NA) in temperature columns can prevent the calculation of thermal comfort indices and compromise the percentile estimates used in cold-wave detection.

The function sus_climate_fill_inmet() implements intelligent gap-filling based on regression models trained with correlated meteorological covariates (air temperature, relative humidity, wind speed, hour of day, seasonality). Filling is performed variable by variable and respects a maximum gap threshold (gap_percentage): if the proportion of missing values in a given series exceeds this threshold, the station is flagged as low quality and no filling is applied.

Main parameters 

df_filled <- sus_climate_fill_inmet(
  df               = df_inmet,
  target_var       = "tair_dry_bulb_c",  # Variável a preencher
  datetime_col     = NULL,     # Detectado automaticamente
  station_col      = NULL,     # Detectado automaticamente
  quality_threshold = 0.4,    # Máximo de NAs para aceitar a série (40%)
  run_evaluation   = FALSE,   # Se TRUE: avalia métricas de ajuste
  gap_percentage   = 0.2,     # Intervalo máximo de gap contínuo a preencher (20%)
  keep_features    = FALSE,   # Manter covariáveis auxiliares no output
  parallel         = TRUE,
  workers          = NULL,    # NULL = detectar automaticamente
  verbose          = TRUE,
  lang             = "pt"
)

Filling the complete dataset

In practice, we apply the filling to each relevant temperature and humidity variable before calculating the thermal comfort indicators:

# Preencher temperatura do ar (bulbo seco)
df_filled <- sus_climate_fill_inmet(
  df         = df_inmet,
  target_var = "tair_dry_bulb_c",
  lang       = "pt",
  verbose    = TRUE
)

# Preencher temperatura máxima e mínima
df_filled <- sus_climate_fill_inmet(df_filled, target_var = "tair_max_c",  lang = "pt")
df_filled <- sus_climate_fill_inmet(df_filled, target_var = "tair_min_c",  lang = "pt")

# Preencher umidade relativa (necessária para UTCI, WBGT, HI)
df_filled <- sus_climate_fill_inmet(df_filled, target_var = "rh_pct",       lang = "pt")

# Verificar proporção de NAs remanescentes
df_filled |>
  summarise(
    n_total    = n(),
    na_tmax    = mean(is.na(tair_max_c)),
    na_tmin    = mean(is.na(tair_min_c)),
    na_tair    = mean(is.na(tair_dry_bulb_c)),
    na_rh      = mean(is.na(rh_pct))
  )

Best practice: Always apply sus_climate_fill_inmet() before sus_climate_compute_coldwaves(). The detection function issues a warning (cli_warn) if it finds NAs in the temperature columns, but it does not fill them automatically — that decision belongs to the analyst, since different imputation strategies can influence the results.

Step 3 — Computing climate indicators

Why go beyond air temperature?

Air temperature (dry bulb) is the most widely available meteorological variable, but it is not the best proxy for human thermal stress under cold conditions. The human body responds to a cold environment resulting from the combination of temperature, humidity, wind speed (wind-chill factor), and radiation. Thermal comfort indices integrate these factors and allow a more realistic estimate of the physiological perception of cold.

The function sus_climate_compute_indicators() calculates the main indices used in the cold-wave detection methodologies implemented in climasus4r. For cold waves, the interest lies in the daily minimum values of these indices:

<div class="feature-icon">🌬️</div>
<h3>UTCI</h3>
<p><strong>Universal Thermal Climate Index.</strong> Reference biometeorological model of ISO 15743. Integrates temperature, humidity, wind, and radiation into an equivalent physiological temperature (°C). In extreme cold, UTCI below −13 °C indicates strong cold stress.</p>
<div class="feature-icon">❄️</div>
<h3>WBGT</h3>
<p><strong>Wet Bulb Globe Temperature.</strong> Operational index widely used in occupational health. Under cold regimes, low WBGT values indicate risk of hypothermia and frostbite injuries in outdoor workers.</p>
<div class="feature-icon">🧊</div>
<h3>HI</h3>
<p><strong>Heat Index.</strong> Although conceived for heat, low values of the daily minimum HI can be used as an indicator of poor thermal comfort under cold and high-humidity conditions.</p>
<div class="feature-icon">🌿</div>
<h3>PET</h3>
<p><strong>Physiological Equivalent Temperature.</strong> Temperature of a reference environment with the same heat exchanges as the body. At negative values, it indicates intense physiological discomfort from cold.</p>

Function call 

df_indicators <- sus_climate_compute_indicators(
  df                   = df_filled,
  indicators           = "all",      # Calcular todos os indicadores disponíveis
  region               = "auto",     # Detectar região automaticamente por metadados
  apply_validity_mask  = TRUE,       # Mascarar valores fora dos limites físicos
  verify_physics       = TRUE,       # Verificar consistência física (Tmin <= Tmean <= Tmax)
  keep_source_vars     = TRUE,       # Manter variáveis originais no output
  verbose              = TRUE,
  lang                 = "pt"
)

# Verificar colunas adicionadas
names(df_indicators) |> grep("utci|wbgt|hi_c|pet", x = _, value = TRUE)

After this step, the data.frame contains the additional columns needed for cold-wave detection by the UTCI, WBGT, and HI methods:

New column Index Unit
utci_c UTCI °C
wbgt_c WBGT °C
hi_c Heat Index °C
pet_c PET °C
utci_c_flag_extreme Hours with UTCI > 38 °C logical
wbgt_c_flag_extreme Hours with WBGT > 32 °C logical
hi_c_flag_extreme Hours with HI > 51 °C logical

UTCI cold-range categories: The ISO 15743 standard defines cold stress categories by UTCI: no thermal stress (≥ 9 °C), slight cold stress (0–9 °C), moderate cold stress (−13 to 0 °C), strong cold stress (−27 to −13 °C), and very strong cold stress (< −27 °C). In cold-wave detection, the UTCI method in climasus4r uses the daily minimum UTCI — the lowest hourly UTCI value recorded that day — compared against the historical P10 of that same indicator.

Step 4 — Cold-wave detection

The sus_climate_compute_coldwaves() function

This is the central function of climasus4r’s cold-detection module. It receives hourly data (the output of sus_climate_compute_indicators()), aggregates them to daily scale, calculates historical percentile thresholds by season of the year (using a sliding window of ±15 days around each day of the year), applies each selected detection methodology, and returns a structured list with three components.

Full signature 

cw_result <- sus_climate_compute_coldwaves(
  df             = df_indicators,   # Output de sus_climate_compute_indicators()
  method         = c("WHO", "WMO", "INMET", "EHF", "UTCI", "WBGT", "HI"),
  baseline_start = "2020-01-01",    # Início do período de referência
  baseline_end   = "2022-12-31",    # Fim do período de referência
  percentile     = 10,              # Percentil para limiares (P10 para cauda fria)
  min_duration   = NULL,            # NULL = usar defaults por método
  lang           = "pt",
  verbose        = TRUE
)

Note on the method = "EHF" argument: The identifier "EHF" is kept for consistency with the heat-wave API, but internally the function applies the Excess Cold Factor (ECF) algorithm — the cold analogue of the EHF. The ECF was proposed by Nairn & Fawcett (2015) and adapted here to detect extreme cold events based on daily mean temperature and an acclimatization factor.

Implemented methodologies

Table 1 presents the seven implemented methodologies, including the base variable, threshold criterion, and default minimum duration.

Table 1 — Cold-wave detection methodologies implemented in sus_climate_compute_coldwaves()

Method Base variable Threshold criterion Minimum duration Reference
WHO Daily Tmin Tmin < P10(Tmin) 3 days WMO & WHO (2015)
WMO Daily Tmin and Tmax Tmin < P10(Tmin) AND Tmax < P10(Tmax) 5 days Perkins & Alexander (2013)
INMET Daily Tmin Tmin < historical mean − 5 °C 5 days INMET (2009)
ECF Daily Tmean ECF > 0 (composite formula; see below) 3 days Nairn & Fawcett (2015)*
UTCI Daily UTCImin UTCImin < P10(UTCImin) 3 days ISO 15743
WBGT Daily WBGTmin WBGTmin < P10(WBGTmin) 3 days Liljegren et al. (2008)
HI Daily HImin HImin < P10(HImin) 3 days Steadman (1979)

*Adaptation for cold: ECF (Excess Cold Factor) instead of EHF (Excess Heat Factor).

Seasonal smoothing of percentiles: For all percentile-based methods, climasus4r uses a sliding window of ±15 days around each day of the year (calculated over the reference period), rather than a fixed percentile calculated over the entire series. This approach, recommended by Fischer & Schär (2010), removes seasonal bias and ensures that the same relative extremity level is detected at any time of year. For cold waves, the percentile is calculated on the lower tail of the distribution (P10), as opposed to the P90 used for heat waves.

Fundamentals of the Excess Cold Factor (ECF)

The ECF is the cold analogue of the EHF (Nairn & Fawcett, 2015). It combines two components that capture, respectively, the absolute magnitude of the cold and the population’s acclimatization factor:

ECF=ECIsig×max⁡(1,ECIacc)\text{ECF} = \text{ECI}_{sig} \times \max(1, \text{ECI}_{acc})

Where:

  • ECI_sig (cold significance index): P5(T‾mean)−T‾3P_5(\bar{T}_{mean}) - \bar{T}_3, measures how much the mean temperature of the last 3 days is below the climatological 5th percentile of the mean temperature. Positive values indicate physiologically relevant cold.
  • ECI_acc (acclimatization index): T‾30−T‾3\bar{T}_{30} - \bar{T}_3, measures how much the mean temperature of the last 3 days is below the average of the preceding 30 days. Positive when the recent period is colder than the previous month — i.e., the body was acclimatized to warmth and was suddenly exposed to cold, amplifying the physiological stress.

The multiplier max⁡(1,ECIacc)\max(1, \text{ECI}_{acc}) ensures that cold events occurring after a relatively warm period receive greater weight — exactly the reverse of the EHF’s logic, where sudden warming amplifies heat risk.

Days with ECF > 0 are classified as cold-wave days. Event intensity is classified into three categories based on the 85th percentile (ECF85) of all positive ECF values observed at the station:

  • Low Intensity (LICW): 0 < ECF_peak < ECF85
  • Severe (SCW): ECF85 ≤ ECF_peak < 3 × ECF85
  • Extreme (ECW): ECF_peak ≥ 3 × ECF85

The INMET method: calibration for cold in Brazil

The INMET cold method defines a cold wave when the daily minimum temperature falls at least 5 °C below the climatological mean of the minimum temperature for 5 or more consecutive days (INMET, 2009). Unlike the heat-wave criterion (which uses maximum temperature), the cold criterion uses the minimum temperature — the variable most sensitive to the penetration of polar air masses.

The climatological mean of Tmin is calculated over the user-defined reference period, using the same ±15-day sliding window used for the percentiles. This criterion is particularly well suited to southern Brazil, where absolute Tmin values are already low and vulnerability to cold-related mortality is more associated with the deviation from the local norm than with the absolute value.

Running the detection

Example 1: air-temperature-based methods 

# Métodos que requerem apenas temperatura do ar (Tmax, Tmin, Tmean)
cw_temp <- sus_climate_compute_coldwaves(
  df             = df_indicators,
  method         = c("WHO", "WMO", "INMET", "EHF"),
  baseline_start = "2020-01-01",
  baseline_end   = "2022-12-31",
  percentile     = 10,
  lang           = "pt",
  verbose        = TRUE
)

Example 2: all methods (including comfort indices) 

# Todos os métodos — requer colunas utci_c, wbgt_c, hi_c
cw_all <- sus_climate_compute_coldwaves(
  df             = df_indicators,
  method         = "all",          # Equivale a c("WHO","WMO","INMET","EHF","UTCI","WBGT","HI")
  baseline_start = "2020-01-01",
  baseline_end   = "2022-12-31",
  percentile     = 10,
  lang           = "pt",
  verbose        = TRUE
)

Example 3: conservative criterion 

# Critério mais conservador: P5 e mínimo de 5 dias para todos os métodos
cw_strict <- sus_climate_compute_coldwaves(
  df             = df_indicators,
  method         = c("WHO", "INMET"),
  baseline_start = "2020-01-01",
  baseline_end   = "2022-12-31",
  percentile     = 5,        # Limiar mais restritivo → menos eventos, mais intensos
  min_duration   = 5,        # Substitui os defaults por método
  lang           = "pt",
  verbose        = TRUE
)

Sensitivity analysis: It is recommended to run the detection with different combinations of percentile (P5, P10, P15) and minimum duration (3, 5, 7 days) and compare the number of detected events. This allows the robustness of epidemiological results to be assessed against methodological choices.

Short baseline in this tutorial: This tutorial uses only 4 years of data (2020–2023) to speed up the download. climasus4r issues a warning when the baseline has fewer than 20 years, which is expected here. For real research, it is recommended to use at least 1981–2010 or 1991–2020 as the climatological reference period.

Output structure

The function returns a named list with three components — the same structure as the output of sus_climate_compute_heatwaves(), but with terminology adapted for cold:

# Inspecionar o output
names(cw_all)
#> [1] "events"  "daily"   "summary"

$events — events table

A data.frame with one row per detected cold-wave event. Each row represents a continuous episode of days with the cold-wave condition active for a given method and station.

# Primeiros eventos detectados
head(cw_all$events)
Column Type Description
event_id character Unique identifier: <station>_<method>_<N>
station_code character INMET station code
method character Detection method (WHO, WMO, etc.)
start_date Date Event start date
end_date Date Event end date
duration_days integer Duration in consecutive days
temp_mean double Mean temperature over the period (method’s variable)
temp_peak double Coldest temperature of the period (minimum)
anomaly_mean double Mean anomaly (threshold − temperature; positive = colder than the threshold)
anomaly_cumulative double Cumulative anomaly over the event
severity_index double Severity index: duration × mean anomaly
ecf_peak double ECF peak (EHF/ECF method only; NA for others)
ecf_mean double Mean ECF during the event (EHF/ECF only)
intensity_class character Classification: LICW, SCW, ECW (EHF/ECF only)
region character Geographic region of the station
federal_unit character State (UF) of the station

Important differences from the heat-wave output:

Field Heat Waves Cold Waves
temp_peak Warmest temperature of the event Coldest temperature of the event
anomaly_mean temp − threshold (positive = warmer) threshold − temp (positive = colder)
Daily flags hw_who, hw_any, … cw_who, cw_any, …
ECF-specific ehf_peak, ehf_mean ecf_peak, ecf_mean
Annual summary total_days_hw total_days_cw
Intensity classes LIHW, SHW, EHW LICW, SCW, ECW 
# Filtrar os 10 eventos mais severos pelo índice de severidade
cw_all$events |>
  arrange(desc(severity_index)) |>
  select(event_id, method, start_date, end_date, duration_days,
         temp_peak, anomaly_mean, severity_index) |>
  head(10)
# Contar eventos por método
cw_all$events |>
  count(method, name = "n_eventos") |>
  arrange(desc(n_eventos))

$daily — daily series with flags

The daily data.frame contains one row per station per day, with aggregated variables and logical (TRUE/FALSE) columns indicating whether that day belongs to a cold wave according to each method:

# Inspecionar colunas de flags
cw_all$daily |>
  select(station_code, date_day, tmin, tmean, starts_with("cw_")) |>
  head(10)

The cw_any column is TRUE if any method detected a cold wave on that day — useful for exposure analyses without commitment to a single criterion.

# Dias com onda de frio ativa por pelo menos um método
cw_all$daily |>
  filter(cw_any == TRUE) |>
  select(date_day, tmin, tmean, cw_who, cw_inmet, cw_ehf, cw_utci) |>
  head(20)
# Concordância entre métodos: proporção de dias classificados por cada um
cw_all$daily |>
  summarise(
    pct_who   = mean(cw_who,   na.rm = TRUE) * 100,
    pct_wmo   = mean(cw_wmo,   na.rm = TRUE) * 100,
    pct_inmet = mean(cw_inmet, na.rm = TRUE) * 100,
    pct_ehf   = mean(cw_ehf,   na.rm = TRUE) * 100,
    pct_utci  = mean(cw_utci,  na.rm = TRUE) * 100,
    pct_wbgt  = mean(cw_wbgt,  na.rm = TRUE) * 100,
    pct_hi    = mean(cw_hi,    na.rm = TRUE) * 100,
    pct_any   = mean(cw_any,   na.rm = TRUE) * 100
  )

$summary — annual summary

The annual summary aggregates statistics by station, method, and year, and is the natural entry point for time-trend analyses:

# Resumo anual
cw_all$summary |>
  filter(method == "INMET") |>
  select(year, station_code, n_events, total_days_cw,
         mean_duration, max_duration, mean_anomaly, severity_total) |>
  arrange(desc(year))
Column Description
year Year
station_code Station code
method Detection method
n_events Number of events in the year
total_days_cw Total cold-wave days in the year
mean_duration Mean duration of events (days)
max_duration Duration of the longest event (days)
mean_intensity Mean temperature during events
max_intensity Peak (coldest) temperature during events
mean_anomaly Mean anomaly during events
severity_total Sum of the events’ severity indices in the year

Step 5 — Visualizing cold waves

The sus_climate_plot_coldwaves() function

Visualization transforms the structured output of sus_climate_compute_coldwaves() into interpretative plots with a cold color palette (blue and violet tones). The function offers four types of visualization, each addressing a different analytical question:

<div class="feature-icon">📅</div>
<h3>timeline</h3>
<p>Gantt-style diagram showing the timing, duration, and intensity of each event. Ideal for identifying prolonged cold episodes in the austral winter and comparing methods.</p>
<div class="feature-icon">🗓️</div>
<h3>calendar</h3>
<p>Calendar heatmap showing the daily occurrence of cold waves across the months. Reveals seasonal concentration (austral winter) and interannual patterns associated with La Niña.</p>
<div class="feature-icon">❄️</div>
<h3>intensity</h3>
<p>Duration × peak minimum temperature scatter plot, with the Y axis inverted (colder = higher). Distinguishes long-lasting events from events with extremely low temperatures.</p>
<div class="feature-icon">📈</div>
<h3>trend</h3>
<p>Grouped bars showing the number of events per year and method. Allows identification of interannual variability and possible trends in cold-wave frequency.</p>

Full signature 

p <- sus_climate_plot_coldwaves(
  cw_result     = cw_all,          # Output de sus_climate_compute_coldwaves()
  type          = "timeline",      # "timeline" | "calendar" | "intensity" | "trend"
  station_code  = NULL,            # Filtrar por estação específica
  method        = NULL,            # Filtrar por método (ex.: "INMET", "EHF")
  year          = NULL,            # Filtrar por ano (útil para "calendar")
  interactive   = TRUE,            # TRUE = plotly; FALSE = ggplot2 estático
  color_palette = "npg",           # Paleta ggsci: "npg", "lancet", "jama", etc.
  lang          = "pt",            # "pt" | "en" | "es"
  save_plot     = NULL             # Caminho para salvar (HTML ou PNG)
)
Parameter Options Effect
type "timeline", "calendar", "intensity", "trend" Plot type
interactive TRUE (plotly), FALSE (ggplot2) Interactivity
color_palette any palette from the ggsci package Color scheme (applied over a base blue palette)
lang "pt", "en", "es" Label language
save_plot .html or .png path Save the plot to disk

Plot 1: Timeline

The timeline plot presents each event as a horizontal segment (Gantt-style), with thickness proportional to duration and color indicating the ECF intensity class (for the EHF/ECF method; for other methods, events are shown in a uniform blue).

# Linha do tempo de todos os eventos — todos os métodos
sus_climate_plot_coldwaves(
  cw_result   = cw_all,
  type        = "timeline",
  interactive = TRUE,
  lang        = "pt"
)
# Filtrar apenas eventos pelo método INMET
sus_climate_plot_coldwaves(
  cw_result   = cw_all,
  type        = "timeline",
  method      = "INMET",
  interactive = TRUE,
  lang        = "pt"
)
# Versão estática para publicação
p_timeline <- sus_climate_plot_coldwaves(
  cw_result     = cw_all,
  type          = "timeline",
  method        = c("WHO", "INMET", "EHF"),
  interactive   = FALSE,        # ggplot2 puro
  color_palette = "lancet",     # Paleta Lancet (jornais biomédicos)
  lang          = "pt",
  save_plot     = "timeline_ondas_frio.png"  # Salvar em PNG
)
print(p_timeline)

Interpretation: Longer segments indicate longer-lasting events; the thickness visually reinforces the duration. Note the concentration of events in June–August (austral winter). The WMO method (dual threshold: Tmin and Tmax < P10) tends to generate fewer, longer-lasting events than the WHO method (Tmin only), since it requires both day and night to be exceptionally cold.

Plot 2: Calendar

The calendar shows each day of the year in colored cells — blue for cold-wave days, gray for normal days. It is the most intuitive plot for communicating the seasonality of events to a non-technical audience.

# Calendário para um ano específico — método WHO
sus_climate_plot_coldwaves(
  cw_result   = cw_all,
  type        = "calendar",
  method      = "WHO",
  year        = 2021,
  interactive = TRUE,
  lang        = "pt"
)
# Calendário com cw_any (qualquer método) — todos os anos
sus_climate_plot_coldwaves(
  cw_result   = cw_all,
  type        = "calendar",
  method      = NULL,          # NULL → usa cw_any (qualquer método)
  interactive = FALSE,
  lang        = "pt"
)

Interpretation: Note the concentration of cold-wave days in June, July, and August in southern Brazil. Years with La Niña events (which tend to intensify cold fronts in RS) show calendars with more consecutive blue blocks. These periods deserve special attention in respiratory and cardiovascular mortality analyses in the SUS.

Plot 3: Intensity vs. duration

This scatter plot positions each event on the duration × peak minimum temperature plane. The Y axis is inverted (scale_y_reverse()), so that lower (colder, more extreme) temperatures appear at the top of the plot — a convention that makes interpretation intuitive: the higher and further right, the greater the epidemiological risk.

# Intensidade ECF (com classificação LICW / SCW / ECW)
sus_climate_plot_coldwaves(
  cw_result   = cw_all,
  type        = "intensity",
  method      = "EHF",         # "EHF" aciona o algoritmo ECF
  interactive = TRUE,
  lang        = "pt"
)
# Todos os métodos juntos (sem classificação de intensidade ECF)
sus_climate_plot_coldwaves(
  cw_result   = cw_all,
  type        = "intensity",
  method      = NULL,
  interactive = FALSE,
  lang        = "pt"
)

Interpretation: Events in the upper-right quadrant (long duration + very low temperature) are the most dangerous from a public health standpoint. The ECF captures the nuance of acclimatization: an event with a Tmin of 5 °C after a well-established winter period is less stressful than the same temperature occurring immediately after warm days — exactly what the ECI_acc component measures.

Plot 4: Annual trend

The trend plot shows the number of events detected per year for each method, allowing an assessment of interannual variability and possible trends in cold-wave frequency over the analyzed period.

# Tendência anual — todos os métodos
sus_climate_plot_coldwaves(
  cw_result   = cw_all,
  type        = "trend",
  interactive = TRUE,
  lang        = "pt"
)
# Tendência apenas para WHO e INMET (comparação de sensibilidade)
sus_climate_plot_coldwaves(
  cw_result   = cw_all,
  type        = "trend",
  method      = c("WHO", "INMET"),
  interactive = FALSE,
  lang        = "pt",
  save_plot   = "tendencia_ondas_frio.png"
)

Interpretation: Interannual variability of cold waves is large and strongly influenced by ENSO (El Niño–Southern Oscillation): La Niña tends to increase the frequency and intensity of cold fronts in southern Brazil. Compare the patterns between methods: the INMET method tends to be more restrictive (requiring a −5 °C deviation from historical Tmin), while the percentile-based methods capture the relativity of the event with respect to the local historical record.

Saving plots 

# Gráfico interativo → arquivo HTML autossuficiente
sus_climate_plot_coldwaves(
  cw_result   = cw_all,
  type        = "timeline",
  interactive = TRUE,
  lang        = "pt",
  save_plot   = "ondas_frio_timeline.html"
)

# Gráfico estático → PNG de alta resolução (300 dpi)
sus_climate_plot_coldwaves(
  cw_result   = cw_all,
  type        = "trend",
  interactive = FALSE,
  lang        = "pt",
  save_plot   = "ondas_frio_tendencia.png"   # ggsave com dpi=300
)

Advanced analysis of the results

Integrating events with the epidemiological calendar

The $daily component with the cw_any column can be directly linked with SUS mortality and morbidity data to calculate excess deaths and hospital admissions during cold waves:

# Exemplo conceitual: cruzamento com dados de mortalidade SIM
# (após completar o pipeline de importação dos dados SIM)

# 1. Preparar a série diária de mortalidade respiratória em idosos

#   filter(
#     cid_grupo %in% c("J"),   # Doenças respiratórias (CIDs J00-J99)
#     idade >= 65               # Idosos - grupo mais vulnerável ao frio
#   )

# 2. Adicionar flag de onda de frio

#     by = c("date" = "date_day")

# 3. Comparar mortalidade em dias com/sem onda de frio

#   )

Exporting events for external analysis 

# Exportar tabela de eventos para CSV
write.csv(
  cw_all$events,
  file         = "eventos_ondas_frio_A801_2020_2023.csv",
  row.names    = FALSE,
  fileEncoding = "UTF-8"
)

# Exportar resumo anual
write.csv(
  cw_all$summary,
  file         = "resumo_anual_ondas_frio_A801.csv",
  row.names    = FALSE,
  fileEncoding = "UTF-8"
)

Concordance analysis between methods 

# Proporção de dias classificados como onda de frio por N métodos simultaneamente
cw_all$daily |>
  mutate(
    n_methods = rowSums(
      across(c(cw_who, cw_wmo, cw_inmet, cw_ehf, cw_utci, cw_wbgt, cw_hi)),
      na.rm = TRUE
    )
  ) |>
  count(n_methods) |>
  mutate(pct = round(n / sum(n) * 100, 1))

Concordance analysis addresses a central question in environmental epidemiology: on how many of the days classified as cold waves is there consensus among the methods? High concordance increases confidence in the results; low concordance suggests that the health impact may vary significantly depending on the criterion adopted.

Cold-related mortality — global epidemiology

  • Gasparrini, A., Guo, Y., Hashizume, M., Lavigne, E., Zanobetti, A., Schwartz, J., … & Armstrong, B. (2015). Mortality risk attributable to high and low ambient temperature: a multicountry observational study. The Lancet, 386(9991), 369–375. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(14)62114-0
  • Huynen, M.M.T.E., Martens, P., Schram, D., Weijenberg, M.P. & Kunst, A.E. (2001). The impact of heat waves and cold spells on mortality rates in the Dutch population. Environmental Health Perspectives, 109(5), 463–470.
  • Basu, R. & Samet, J.M. (2002). Relation between elevated ambient temperature and mortality: a review of the epidemiologic evidence. Epidemiologic Reviews, 24(2), 190–202.

Brazil and southern-region context

  • Braga, A.L.F., Zanobetti, A. & Schwartz, J. (2001). The time course of weather-related deaths. Epidemiology, 12(6), 662–667.
  • Vasconcelos, J., Freire, E., Morais, J., Machado, J.R. & Santana, P. (2013). The health impacts of poor housing conditions and thermal discomfort. Procedia Environmental Sciences, 19, 107–112.

General concepts and percentile framework

  • Perkins, S.E. & Alexander, L.V. (2013). On the measurement of heat waves. Journal of Climate, 26(13), 4500–4517.
  • Fischer, E.M. & Schär, C. (2010). Consistent geographical patterns of changes in high-impact European heatwaves. Nature Geoscience, 3, 398–403.

WHO and WMO methods (adapted for cold)

  • WMO & WHO (2015). Heatwaves and Health: Guidance on Warning-System Development. World Meteorological Organization, Geneva.
  • WMO (2021). Guidelines on the Definition and Monitoring of Extreme Weather and Climate Events. World Meteorological Organization.

INMET method

  • INMET — Instituto Nacional de Meteorologia (2009). Normais Climatológicas do Brasil 1961–1990. Brasília: MAPA/INMET.

ECF (Excess Cold Factor)

  • Nairn, J.R. & Fawcett, R.J.B. (2015). The Excess Heat Factor: A metric for heatwave intensity and its use in classifying heatwave severity. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health, 12(1), 227–253. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph120100227

UTCI (Universal Thermal Climate Index) — cold regime

  • Broede, P., Fiala, D., Blazejczyk, K., Holmer, I., Jendritzky, G., Kampmann, B., Tinz, B. & Havenith, G. (2012). Deriving the operational procedure for the Universal Thermal Climate Index (UTCI). International Journal of Biometeorology, 56(3), 481–494. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00484-011-0454-1
  • ISO 15743:2008. Ergonomics of the thermal environment — Cold workplaces: Risk assessment and management. International Organization for Standardization.

WBGT (Wet Bulb Globe Temperature)

  • Liljegren, J.C., Carhart, R.A., Lawday, P., Tschopp, S. & Sharp, R. (2008). Modeling the wet bulb globe temperature using standard meteorological measurements. Journal of Occupational and Environmental Hygiene, 5(10), 645–655.

HI (Heat Index)

  • Steadman, R.G. (1984). A universal scale of apparent temperature. Journal of Applied Meteorology and Climatology, 23(12), 1674–1687.
